historical_record.description: Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 112, Rothschild House.
After the Rothschilds the house was long a rooming house and then apartments, until its restoration as a single house from 1974.
Water service was applied for at the house in August 1880.

The house was a restrained Italianate wood-frame dwelling of two living floors over a ground-level basement, with slanted bays, a portico on Corinthian columns and a bracketed cornice, in an R-4 district with a 130-E height limit inside Redevelopment Area A-2. By October 1974 the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency had designated the house, as part of a longer row, for rehabilitation in place for exceptional historical and architectural merit. The City Planning Commission unanimously refused to designate the Rothschild House a city landmark at that time, leaving it open to reconsideration after restoration.

On the Landmarks Preservation Advisory Board's recommendation, the City Planning Commission unanimously proposed the Rothschild House to the Board of Supervisors for designation as a city landmark (Resolution 8504).

notable_residents.name: Hugo Rothschild
notable_residents.detail: Hugo Rothschild, a German-born confectioner who with George Ehrenpfort ran the Rothschild-Ehrenpfort candy factory, took water here in August 1880 and owned and lived in the house with his family until 1902; his daughter Henriette was the first wife of the anthropologist Alfred Kroeber.

unknowns: The landmark designation is dated 1979 in the Article 10 record, but the City Planning Commission's recommendation that the Board of Supervisors designate the Rothschild House was voted on 21 February 1980.
